newsitem.title: USA: Tough-talking U.S. Cyprus envoy forged Bosnia deal.
newsitem.headline: Tough-talking U.S. Cyprus envoy forged Bosnia deal.

text.p: Richard Holbrooke, the tough-talking U.S. envoy who forged a peace agreement in Bosnia, is back in the diplomatic saddle to try to promote a settlement on the divided island of Cyprus.

Holbrooke was recalled by the Clinton administration from a finance industry job on Wednesday to reinvigorate U.S. efforts to bring together the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, a task that has defied peacemakers for more than 20 years.

His appointment as special presidential emissary for Cyprus, hailed by the State Department as "a rebirth and a renewal" of U.S. policy in the region, inevitably fuelled high expectations of a breakthrough in the intractable dispute.

The former assistant secretary of state is best known as the architect of the Balkan peace agreement hammered out in Dayton, Ohio, in November 1995. A tough negotiator renowned for straight talk, Holbrooke cajoled and bullied the leaders of former Yugoslavia into ending the 43-month-long conflict and reluctantly creating a two-part Bosnian state.
But three months later he left government service to work for investment bank Credit Suisse First Boston in New York. He said he wanted to be closer to his family, who live there.

Holbrooke's last diplomatic effort before resigning from the State Department was to have been a crack at the Cyprus problem, but he abandoned the bid after an upsurge in tension between Greece and Turkey.

Several further disappointments followed after he moved to New York. He failed to win last year's Nobel Peace Prize for the Bosnia accord and was later passed over for the posts of secretary of state and U.N. ambassador in the second Clinton administration, which took office in January.

Holbrooke claimed to be a reluctant participant in the turmoil of the Balkans. When he first took his job as assistant secretary of state for European and Canadian affairs in 1994, he told visitors that Bosnia was a hopeless case that he planned to have as little to do with as possible.

But a loss of military momentum by the previously dominant Bosnian Serbs, combined with a new tougher Balkan policy by the Clinton administration, enabled him to start a peace mission in August 1995 that led eventually to Dayton.
It was Holbrooke's decision to stage the talks at the austere Wright-Patterson airbase in Dayton. He calculated that the Balkan leaders would not want to stay there a minute longer than they had to.
Colleagues say Holbrooke will pull out all the stops to get a job done. One British official said he could "behave like a bull in a china shop. And he frequently does."
The 56-year-old New Yorker has a reputation for mincing no words. He once described Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, a key figure in the Bosnia negotiations, as "not a nice man."

A tall man with horn-rimmed glasses, Holbrooke was eager to brief the media during his Balkan travels, leading envious colleagues to joke that "the most dangerous place in Bosnia is between Richard Holbrooke and a television camera."

Holbrooke was U.S. ambassador to Germany beginning in July 1993 until Clinton recalled him to Washington a year later. He is no stranger to negotiations, having cut his teeth as a backroom aide in the U.S. delegation to the Paris peace talks on Vietnam in 1968-69. Before that he was special assistant for Vietnam to President Lyndon Johnson in 1966 and 1967.

Holbrooke was born April 24, 1941, in New York City. He joined the foreign service in 1962 after graduating from Brown University. From 1985 until his appointment in Germany, he was managing director of New York investment firm Lehman Brothers.

He is a favourite subject of gossip columnists. His 1995 wedding to Kati Marton, a journalist and former wife of ABC television anchor Peter Jennings, was the talk of the capital. It was his third marriage. He has two sons from his first, to Washington lawyer Larrine Sullivan.
